## Week 7: tuning and regularization

Every method so far had a knob. This week chooses it by $K$-fold cross-validation, with the curve it draws against $\lambda$, $k$ and tree depth, and the standard error of a held-out score. Then what the choice costs: from the bias--variance decomposition, the error of $k$-nearest neighbors in $d$ dimensions, the rate $n^{-2/(d+2)}$, and what an assumption buys (an additive truth, a sparse one). Ridge and the lasso side by side in the simplest design: shrinkage against soft thresholding, and selection against prediction; the smoothing penalty on a spline as ridge with weights. What changes when $p > n$: the minimum-norm interpolant, which zero-error fit you get, and the double-descent curve.

**Reading**

- ISLR Chapter 5 (Resampling Methods), section 5.1, pp. 197–209: the validation set, leave-one-out and $K$-fold cross-validation, and the bias--variance trade-off in choosing $K$. Skim 5.1.5 (classification), pp. 206–208. Section 5.2, the bootstrap, is not needed this week.
- ISLR Chapter 6, section 6.2.3, pp. 250–252 (choosing the tuning parameter by cross-validation), picking up where the last reading stopped. Re-read "A simple special case for ridge regression and the lasso", pp. 247–249: the lecture works in that design.
- ISLR Chapter 6, section 6.4, pp. 261–267 (what changes when $p > n$). Section 6.3, which sits between them, is not part of the course.
- ISLR Chapter 7, section 7.5.1, pp. 301–302 (smoothing splines: a penalty on wiggliness instead of a basis size). Skim 7.5.2, pp. 302–304.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), "Generalization gap" and "Overparameterization: empirical phenomena", pp. 100–104 (the double-descent curve, and why it is not universal); ISLR section 10.8, pp. 439–443 (interpolation and double descent, with the natural-spline example the lecture demonstrates); ISLR section 3.5, pp. 105–110, re-read (what happens to $k$-nearest neighbors as the number of inputs grows).

Deeper: ESL section 7.10.2, pp. 245–247 (the wrong and the right way to do cross-validation, which the seminar meets); ESL section 2.5, pp. 22–28 (local methods in high dimensions); ESL sections 3.4.1–3.4.3, pp. 61–73 (ridge and the lasso in general designs); Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal, "Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias--variance trade-off", *PNAS* 116(32), 2019; Györfi, Kohler, Krzyżak and Walk, *A Distribution-Free Theory of Nonparametric Regression* (2002), Chapter 6, and Stone, *Annals of Statistics* 1982, for the rigorous and the minimax form of the nearest-neighbor rate the lecture derives from a stated lemma.

**Lecture:** [slides](weeks/07-regularization-highdim/slides/07-1-regularization.html)

**Seminar:** released here at the start of the week. A cross-validation pipeline on the Spotify tracks ([data note](data/spotify.html)); learning curves for $k$-nearest neighbors in one, two, five and ten dimensions, read against the rate; then, after cross-validation has worked for you, two ways it goes wrong: duplicated tracks on both sides of a fold, and a random split against a split in time.
